data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A decentralized network is more resilient to correlated failure iff its operational diversity exceeds the marginal redundancy of a large service. Redundancy within a single system does not increase if every redundant unit shares the same latent cause; only operational diversity decouples failure.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If small services are operationally homogeneous (same framework, cloud provider, dependency), decentralization provides no resilience benefit.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service has diverse internal sub-organizations and strictly separated stacks, it may achieve the same decoupling as a decentralized network.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If operational diversity is shown to correlate with failure in a non-monotonic way (e.g., increasing fragility due to integration complexity), the claim inverts.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In a large service with strictly more redundancy, every replica shares the same CI/CD pipeline, config store, and organizational process. A latent defect (e.g., bad deployment) is a shared cause waiting to activate; redundancy does not reduce its probability. A decentralized network is resilient only when its small services have heterogeneous stacks, processes, and domains. We model systemic survival as requiring both unit-level redundancy AND independence of latent causes. If all units share latent causes, systemic failure collapses to a single point of failure. Therefore, strict internal redundancy provides no protection against shared causes; only diversity (which decentralization allows but does not guarantee) does.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
